title: Choose the bolder editor-centered layout
question: Which fresh arrangement best puts the note first while keeping the workbench practical?

options.label: Buffer-led editor
options.thesis: Treat the active note as the workbench: a compact buffer strip identifies open context, while the editor owns nearly the full screen.
options.viewport: Desktop: full-width workspace header, note buffer strip above a centered editor, file tree available from Browse, and a crisp Vim-style statusline. Mobile: editor first with touch-sized Browse and New note actions; Vim mode UI stays hidden.
options.risk: Tabs must represent real notes and remain usable when the workspace contains many files.

options.label: Editor with right-hand navigator
options.thesis: Lead with the writing canvas and place the note tree at the far edge, so the workspace reads editor-first at a glance.
options.viewport: Desktop: a wide left-aligned editor with compact file navigation on the right and a full-width statusline. Mobile: editor first with a labeled Browse drawer and touch actions; no Vim mode controls.
options.risk: A right-side tree may feel unfamiliar to people expecting left navigation.

options.label: Editor over a note shelf
options.thesis: Reserve the upper workspace for writing and keep note navigation in a shallow bottom shelf, inspired by an editor’s lower pane.
options.viewport: Desktop: editor occupies the upper workbench, a compact note shelf sits below, and status remains at the bottom edge. Mobile: shelf becomes a touch-scrollable browse row; mode labels and keyboard-only controls are absent.
options.risk: A bottom shelf competes with the editor’s vertical reading space.
